faq.q: Why does the talus have a high risk of avascular necrosis?

exam: What immediate step should you take when a patient presents with a suspected talar neck fracture? — Immobilise the ankle, assess neurovascular status, and arrange urgent imaging.
How does the retrograde blood supply of the talus influence management of a fracture? — Highlights need for early reduction and careful monitoring for AVN; avoid prolonged displacement.
Which ligament provides medial stability to the talus and how would you test it? — Deltoid ligament; perform valgus stress test with the ankle in slight dorsiflexion.
In a low‑resource setting without CT, how would you decide between conservative and surgical treatment? — Use X‑ray displacement criteria (>2 mm) and clinical instability to guide referral.

What distinguishes a talar body fracture from a calcaneal fracture on plain film? — Talus fracture shows disruption of the ankle mortise and may have a visible neck line; calcaneus fracture shows a broken calcaneal tuberosity.
Why is an open talar fracture an emergency? — Risk of infection, skin loss, and rapid loss of blood supply requiring prompt debridement and antibiotics.
What long‑term complication should you counsel a patient after a talar neck fracture? — Post‑traumatic arthritis and possible AVN requiring future arthrodesis.
How would you assess for subtalar joint involvement in a talar injury? — Test inversion/eversion range; pain or block suggests subtalar involvement.
ai.title: Talus Anatomy and Clinical Relevance
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The talus is the central ankle bone with no muscular attachments and a retrograde blood supply, making it vulnerable to avascular necrosis after fractures. Understanding its relations, blood supply, and common injuries is essential for low‑resource settings.

b: Prone to osteonecrosis after neck fracture
sections.p: The talus transmits body weight from the tibia to the foot and allows dorsiflexion and plantarflexion. It is unique because it has no muscle insertions and relies entirely on ligaments for stability.

b: Neck is the narrowest region, common fracture site
sections.p: The talus sits between the tibia/fibula superiorly and the calcaneus inferiorly. It has three main parts: head, neck, and body, with the trochlear surface articulating with the tibia.

b: Ligaments: deltoid (medial), lateral collateral, spring ligament (calcaneonavicular)
sections.p: Anteriorly the talus contacts the navicular via the talonavicular joint; posteriorly it contacts the calcaneus at the subtalar joint; medially it is bounded by the medial malleolus, laterally by the fibula.

b: Vulnerability: fracture can disrupt flow → avascular necrosis
In low‑resource settings, rely on clinical signs of necrosis
sections.p: The talus receives a retrograde blood supply mainly from the artery of the tarsal canal, the artery of the sinus tarsi, and branches of the posterior tibial artery. The neck is a watershed zone.

b: Pain after injury follows these dermatomes
sections.p: Sensory innervation comes from the tibial nerve (medial side) and the deep peroneal nerve (lateral side). No motor nerves are involved because there are no muscles attached.
The talus transfers load from the tibia to the foot while permitting smooth dorsiflexion and plantarflexion. Its smooth trochlear surface distributes forces evenly across the ankle joint.

b: Talar neck fracture → risk of AVN, post‑traumatic arthritis
Subtalar dislocation → check for skin compromise
sections.p: Fractures of the talar neck or body are high‑energy injuries common in road‑traffic accidents. Because of limited blood flow, avascular necrosis (AVN) is a major complication. Dislocations may accompany fractures and threaten neurovascular structures.

t.b: Detect fracture line and displacement; if unavailable, use clinical swelling, deformity, and inability to bear weight
Defines fracture pattern for surgical planning; if unavailable, rely on detailed X‑ray interpretation
Shows bone marrow edema indicating early AVN; if unavailable, monitor for persistent pain and collapse on follow‑up X‑ray

b: Positive talar neck tenderness with limited dorsiflexion suggests fracture
Absent posterior tibial pulse after dislocation warrants urgent reduction
sections.p: At the bedside, assess ankle range of motion, compare swelling, and test for tenderness over the talar neck. Look for skin tenting, neurovascular status, and ability to plantar‑flex.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe ankle deformity with loss of pulse
Increasing pain despite immobilisation, suggesting AVN
